1.pericope_label: Elisha promises plenty within a day, and the officer on whose hand the king leaned scoffs at it

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the division of the chapters unfortunate, there being no break in the story, and takes the prophet to be addressing the king and the attendants present. He renders the seah the most usual corn measure and insists the oracle is far more abrupt in the original than in English, adding, against Thenius, that the barley was meant for human food as barley cakes and not only as fodder, and explaining the gate by trade, the corn market being held just within it. The scoffer he makes an adjutant, or aide-de-camp, or esquire, comparing the phrase about the hand leaned upon with the expression used of Naaman; the scoff itself he will render either as a concession, that even granting Jehovah should make windows in the sky the cheapness can hardly ensue so soon, or as a question put to a statement, but in any case the tone is that of scoffing unbelief, as Reuss renders it with French point. Elisha’s answer, he notes, partly imitates the scoffer’s own words.

Clarke makes the word a reply to the desponding language of the king at the close of the preceding chapter, vindicating the prophet from the charge of having caused the calamity; he reckons the seah at about two gallons and a half and the shekel at two shillings and fourpence at the lowest computation, remarking on the wide difference between this and the price of the ass’s head named before, and says the Hebrew name of the scoffer’s office occurs often and seems to point out one of the highest in the state. On the sentence passed he dissents sharply: this was a mere prediction of the man’s death and not a judgment for his unbelief, since any person in his circumstances might have spoken as he did, and any person in his place might have been trodden to death in the gate; what he said was that nothing but a miracle could procure such plenty, and by a miracle alone was it done. Wesley gives the measure as six cabs, or about a peck and pottle of our measure, which is the same amount by another road.

Henry draws the timing into a rule: the king despaired and grew weary of waiting, and then Elisha foretold it, when things were at the worst, for man’s extremity is God’s opportunity of magnifying his power, and his time to appear for his people is when their strength is gone; and though the king had just threatened the prophet’s life, God promises to save it, and his people with him, for where sin abounded grace doth much more abound. He thinks the scoffer held the thing impossible unless God should rain corn out of the clouds as he once rained manna. The death he calls the just doom of the man’s infidelity, that he should see the plenty for his conviction and yet not eat of it to his comfort, unbelief being a sin by which men dishonour God and deprive themselves of the favours he designed for them; and as the murmuring Israelites saw Canaan and could not enter in, so, after bishop Patrick, will it be with those who believe not the promise of eternal life.

Gill insists the leaning was not figurative, not merely that the king confided in the man, but literal, the king resting on his hand and being supported by him as a form and matter of state. He adds that the title marks a principal lord, the third to the king; that the word the Septuagint uses is interpreted by Suidas of those holding three spears together; and that the like state was kept by the king of Syria and by the kings and queens of Persia.

debates.question: Was the officer’s death a judgment on his unbelief?

positions.view: Yes: the just doom of his infidelity, to see the plenty for his conviction and not taste it
No: a mere prediction of his death, since any man in his circumstances might have spoken so, and any man in his post might have been trodden down

debates.question: How large was the measure the prophet named?

positions.view: About two gallons and a half
Six cabs, about a peck and pottle, which comes to the same
Simply the most usual corn measure, without reduction to English units

outliers.claim: Alone in pressing that the leaning was literal court ceremony, and in bringing Suidas and the Persian and Syrian courts to the officer’s title.
Alone in denying that the man’s death was a judgment at all, against the whole weight of the devotional reading.

themes: To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel in the gate of Samaria
Then a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God
Behold, if the Lord would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?
Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof

3.pericope_label: Four lepers reason themselves into the Syrian camp, find it deserted, and carry the news to the gate

schools.summary: Clarke passes on the rabbinic tradition flatly, that the Gemara in Sota and Jarchi and others say these four were Gehazi and his three sons, adding that at the entering in of the gate means they were not suffered to mingle in society. Of the panic he says only that the noise threw the Syrians into confusion, since they imagined powerful auxiliaries had been hired against them, and of the flight that the advanced guards should have been where the lepers found nobody. Wesley takes the names in the Syrians’ cry to be real: under the name of the Hittites, as elsewhere under that of the Amorites, all the people of Canaan are meant, many spared or fled on Joshua’s coming to the bordering lands, where they grew powerful; and the kings of the Egyptians means either the king of Egypt, the plural put for the singular, or the princes and governors of the several provinces.

Gill reports the same tradition about the lepers and explains the place: lepers being obliged by law to be outside the city and camp, these may have had a dwelling assigned near the gate, or got as near as they could, partly for relief, partly for fear of the Syrians; and their proposal to enter the city would have been contrary to the law that forbade them. On the noise he offers three possibilities, that it was made in the air by angels, or that the Lord so wrought on their imagination that they fancied they heard it, or that he caused the noise in their ears, calling it the noise of many armies with the Targum. On the lepers’ change of mind he puts the scruple plainly: it was not right to take the booty to themselves, not just to their brethren, and might not prove well to themselves in the issue.

Henry half accepts the tradition, that perhaps Gehazi was one of the four, which might be why the king noticed him afterwards, and he makes the exclusion providential, Samaria being delivered and not knowing it, so that four men shut out as unclean became its intelligencers. He lays the lepers’ options side by side and concludes that common prudence puts us upon the method that may better our condition but cannot make it worse. He insists the deliverance came not by might or power but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts, with no sword drawn and no blood shed, and reads the Syrians’ cry as self-deception, since as they were imposed upon by the sound, so they imposed upon themselves by the interpretation they made of it. On the plunder he has them correct themselves, that they do not well to conceal good tidings from the community they belong to under colour of being avenged for their exclusion, since the law did that and not the people; and the news was not the less acceptable for being first brought by lepers.

Ellicott will have none of the tradition, noting the ascription to Rashi with an exclamation and nothing more, and explaining the lepers’ plight without it: nobody brought them food any longer, owing to the famine. He keeps to the words, that to fall unto is to desert, that if they save us alive means and give us food for pity’s sake, and that the qualifying but is absent from the Hebrew. Against Henry he answers the Syrians’ cry with history, the tract of north Syria between the Euphrates and the Orontes being the cradle of the Hittite race, over which these kings of the several tribes bore sway, their power once reaching over much of Asia Minor as inscriptions prove. He explains the burying of the spoil as a common practice of Orientals, with whom holes in the ground or the wall serve for banks, and renders the lepers’ fear literally: guilt will find us.

debates.question: Were the kings of the Hittites and of the Egyptians real powers, or a panic-invention?

positions.view: An invention of their own fright: there was for aught we know but one king of Egypt, and what kings there were of the Hittites nobody can imagine
Real dynasts: the Hittite kings of north Syria, whose power once reached over much of Asia Minor
The surviving Canaanite peoples under an old name, and the provincial governors of Egypt

debates.question: Were the four lepers Gehazi and his sons?

positions.view: So the Jewish authorities say, reported without comment
Perhaps: Gehazi may have been one, which would explain the king noticing him later
Not worth entertaining; the famine explains their situation without it

outliers.claim: Alone in bringing Hittite and Assyrian history and rock inscriptions to bear on what the Syrians thought they heard.
Alone in distinguishing three ways the noise could have been produced: made in the air by angels, impressed on the imagination, or caused in the ears.

themes: there were four leprous men at the entering in of the gate: and they said one to another, Why sit we here until we die?
let us fall unto the host of the Syrians: if they save us alive, we shall live; and if they kill us, we shall but die
the Lord had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses
Lo, the king of Israel hath hired against us the kings of the Hittites, and the kings of the Egyptians
We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace

12.pericope_label: The king suspects an ambush, a servant proposes the last horses, and the scouts track the flight toward Jordan

schools.summary: Clarke calls the king’s conclusion a very natural one and credits him with a noble defence, sharing the sufferings of the besieged and ever at his post, since even in vile Ahab there were some good things. On the servant’s speech he takes the boldest line of any voice here: the verse is very difficult, and with Kennicott he judges seven Hebrew words a careless scribal repetition improperly continued in the text, absent from the Septuagint and the Syriac, wanting in more than forty manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, unpointed in some and blotted out in others, so that the verse should be read without them; and he renders the closing words not consumed but perfect, that is fit for service. Of the horses actually sent he supposes they found on examination that only two were effective, though if two chariots went each would have had its pair. The litter on the road he calls manifest proof of the hurry and precipitancy of the flight. Wesley emends nothing, taking the Hebrew prefix not as a note of similitude but as an affirmation of certainty, so that the servant says the horses are of a truth all the multitude of the horses of Israel that are left; the verse deserved its double behold, to show what the famine had done to men and beasts alike, and to what a low ebb the king was come.

Ellicott quotes Grotius, that misery is suspicious, and allows that stratagems such as this king suspected are common in warfare. He keeps the difficult verse as it stands, reading its repetition as dwelling pathetically on the fewness of the survivors, and finds in it two contingencies supposed by the adviser, that the horses and their drivers may return safe and share the fortune of those who are left, or be taken and slain and so be even as all the multitude that are consumed; the servant, he says, is no more sanguine than his master. He allows that Reuss may instead be right in finding only a natural doubt whether starving animals are adequate to the service required, consumed then meaning spent. Against the others he takes five as an indefinite small number, like our half a dozen, and reads the Hebrew of the next verse as teams for two chariots, sent so that if attacked they might make a better resistance, or so that if one were captured the other might escape with the news; and he holds the scouts went not to Jordan itself, at least twenty miles off, but in the direction of it.

Henry grants the facts of the king’s fear and turns them inward: he knew he had no reason to expect God should appear thus wonderfully for him, having forfeited his favour by unbelief and impatience, and knew no reason the Syrians had to fly, since neither he nor any attendant seems to have heard the noise that frightened them; a guilty conscience fears the worst and makes men suspicious. He notes that the adviser was very sensible of the deplorable condition of the people, repeating of the horses that they are as all the multitude of Israel, which used to glory in their numbers and was now diminished and brought low; that it should seem there were only two horses fit to be sent, and those chariot-horses; and that the Syrians could be tracked by the garments they threw off for speed.

Gill notes that the king rose upon the report made to him, that the five horses proposed were those that had not died through the famine as the rest had, and that the two actually taken were the best, perhaps those that drew the king’s own chariot, and so better fed and fitter for the expedition. On the pursuit he holds that the scouts, not finding the Syrians in the camp and knowing the route they would take to their own land, went as far as Jordan, over which they must pass.

debates.question: Is the repeated clause in the servant’s speech a scribal interpolation?

positions.view: Yes: seven words carelessly repeated, absent from the versions and from more than forty manuscripts, and to be deleted
No: the Hebrew prefix is not a note of similitude but an affirmation of certainty, and the sentence stands
No: the repetition dwells pathetically on the fewness of the survivors, and only one stray article is a transcriber’s error

debates.question: Why were two horses sent when five were asked for?

positions.view: Because only two were fit: the rest were dead, eaten, or too weak for the journey
Because five was never a literal count but an indefinite small number, and two teams were sent for safety’s sake

debates.question: How far did the scouts go?

positions.view: As far as Jordan itself, over which the Syrians had to pass
Not to the river, which is twenty miles off, but in its direction

outliers.claim: Alone in emending the text, setting out the manuscript evidence of Kennicott and De Rossi and printing the verse without the repeated words.
Alone in denying that only two horses were available, by taking five as an indefinite number and the pair of teams as a tactical choice.

themes: I will now shew you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we be hungry
Let some take, I pray thee, five of the horses that remain, which are left in the city
behold, they are as all the multitude of Israel that are left in it
They took therefore two chariot horses; and the king sent after the host of the Syrians
all the way was full of garments and vessels, which the Syrians had cast away in their haste

16.pericope_label: The camp is spoiled, the price falls as the prophet said, and the scoffer is trodden down in the gate

schools.summary: Gill says the people spoiled the tents of their riches and their provisions, of which there was such plenty that it served not only for present use but for sale, which is how the price came down as the prophet had said. The gate-keeping commission he explains by the circumstances: it was not to keep out an enemy, of which there was now no danger, but to prevent disorders and tumults among the people, that they might go out in an orderly and regular manner. Of the closing verses he says the words spoken to the king and to the lord are set down again so that it might be observed how exactly the prophecies were fulfilled.

Ellicott corrects the word, that what was spoiled was the camp rather than the tents, and reads the appointment as a pluperfect, now the king had appointed him, to maintain order as the famished crowd poured out of the city. He follows Thenius in a detail that makes the death worse, that the trampling probably happened as the crowd was returning from the Syrian camp, wild with excess of food and drink after their long abstinence, and that the man was trampled down while trying to discharge his duty, so that he saw the plenty with his eyes and did not eat thereof; he notes that Reuss takes the charge of the gate to be the charge of the market, the market being held on the space adjoining the gate. Of the repetition he says the author sets down the prediction and its fulfilment with obvious satisfaction and that the moral is a warning against unbelief, while suspecting that the phrase who spake is a spurious repetition, wanting in some Hebrew manuscripts and in the Syriac and the Vulgate and the Arabic.

Clarke supplies the mechanics of the death: the people rushing out to get spoil and in again to carry it to their houses, the officer set over the gate was borne down by the multitude and trodden to death. He draws the moral from the accuracy rather than the horror, that this too was foreseen by the spirit of prophecy, and that the literal and exact fulfilment of such predictions must have acquired the prophet a great deal of credit in Israel; and he sets the whole episode within Lightfoot’s year-by-year reckoning of the reign, in the fifth year of Jehoram, when Samaria was besieged by Ben-hadad and after being nearly destroyed by famine was suddenly relieved. Wesley states the warning itself: see how heinously God resents our distrust of his power, providence and promise, for whenever God promises the end, he knows where to provide the means.

debates.question: At what point in the rush was the officer trampled?

positions.view: In the press of the crowd going out for spoil and coming back in with it
On the return, when they came back from the camp wild with excess of food and drink after long abstinence

outliers.claim: Alone in placing the siege and its relief within a year-by-year chronology of the reign, drawn from Lightfoot, which fixes it in the fifth year.
Alone in dating the trampling to the crowd’s return from the camp, gorged after long abstinence, on Thenius’s suggestion.
